Question: A non-zero digit is chosen in such a way that the probability of choosing digit \(d\) is \(\log_{10}(d+1)-\log_{10}d.\) The probability that the digit \(2\) is chosen is exactly \(\frac{1}{2}\) the probability that the digit chosen is in the set
Solution:
Each listed set contains consecutive digits, so adding its probabilities makes the intermediate logarithms cancel. Let \(D\) denote the chosen digit. Since different digit outcomes are mutually exclusive, for \(1\le r\le s\le9\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(r\le D\le s)
&=(\log_{10}(r+1)-\log_{10}r)+\cdots\\
&\quad +(\log_{10}(s+1)-\log_{10}s)\\
&=\log_{10}\frac{s+1}{r}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The desired set must have probability twice that of digit \(2\), namely
\[
2P(D=2)=2\log_{10}\frac32
=\log_{10}\frac94.
\]
For digits \(4\) through \(8\), the endpoint ratio is \((8+1)/4=9/4\), exactly as required. The endpoint ratios for choices A through E are \(2,5/3,9/4,2,5/2\); only C has the required ratio. Therefore the set is \(\boxed{\{4,5,6,7,8\}}\), choice C.
